clear and familiar; he has illuminated it with the light of his
thought and moulded it by his achievements. In the dark
primaeval forest in which man as it were first finds himself,
he begins to adapt things to his basic needs; he introduces
light and order into nature whose powers he observes and
subdues to his own purposes. The circle widens itself more
and more until it at last becomes so extensive that the
darkness of the world recedes into remotest distance and man
loses sight of the element of mystery. Thus he has no longer
any reason to erect an altar to the "unknown God". But has
he been able at the same time to efface the fear of life which
lay behind the belief in the "unknown God"? Or does it
only lurk secretly at the heart of his life, stilled by his busy
activities or hidden by the veil of a stupendous illusion, only
to cry out more loudly at times? Has then man really become
master of his world and his life? Have the world and
existence in truth lost their uncanny and mysterious elements
in consequence of the powerful organization of human culture
and civilization? And do there not still remain, in the inner
life of man, mysterious forces which as it were are only
waiting for the moment when they can spring forth with
daemonic energy?
When Paul says: "What therefore you worship as un-
known, this I proclaim to you"
he is admitting that in the
cultic worship springing from anxiety an element of truth
is contained. Such a cult implies the search for the one true
God, because it implies the awareness that man is not his
own master. Man will never be freed from anxiety by seeking
to illuminate the world, by seeking to control and organize
it in his own interests, but only by facing the question which
his anxiety suggests, by giving due recognition to his religious
awareness, so that it may ultimatély lead him to the know-
ledge of the one God who is Lord of heaven and earth. This
question is well illustrated by a poem of the young Nietzsche:
